This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the <term>copyright</term> <note>The legal right that grants the creator of an original work exclusive rights to its use and distribution.</note> to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain</term> <note>Works that are no longer protected by copyright and are free for anyone to use.</note>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary from country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture, and knowledge that is often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations, and other marginalia <note>Handwritten notes or marks made in the margins of a book by previous readers or librarians.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying <note>The use of software programs to automatically search or download data at high speeds.</note>.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files:* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying:* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system. If you are conducting research on machine translation, <term>optical character recognition</term> <note>Also known as OCR; the technology used to convert images of text into machine-readable data.</note>, or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution:* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal:* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we cannot offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About Google Book Search

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. # PREFACE

### TO THE

## FIRST EDITION.

---

I submit the following pages for public review with significant hesitation and great modesty <note>original: "diffidence"</note>.

The subject is largely unrelated to my usual professional duties <note>original: "avocations"</note>. I originally took it up simply as a matter of curiosity, though in my estimation, its importance later grew considerably. However, I am naturally aware of my own lack of the scientific knowledge required to explain <note>original: "elucidate"</note> the specific goal of my current research. Because of this, I have long felt an anxious desire that someone better qualified by their professional career—and more competent in every other respect—had been persuaded to take on the task that has now fallen to me. But see—

<page-num>xii</page-num>
->PREFACE TO THE<-

Having no immediate prospect of this hope being fulfilled, and having been frequently asked for information by both medical professionals and others, I have, at last, felt almost compelled to present a brief overview of the progress made so far in explaining <note>original: "elucidation"</note> this mysterious <note>original: "obscure"</note> but most interesting subject. As the reader will soon see, this could not have been done satisfactorily through just casual and interrupted conversation. Indeed, it is almost impossible for anyone to understand many of the necessary details without having either conducted experiments themselves or witnessed—or at least carefully studied—those performed by others.

Fortunately, a highly respected friend, whose active and enlightened mind is constantly attentive to the interests of literature and science, has recently given me an excellent opportunity to introduce the subject to the British public by sharing with me the recent Report on the Magnetic Experiments <term>Magnetic Experiments: In this context, this refers to "Animal Magnetism" or Mesmerism, a 19th-century theory involving an invisible natural force (magnetism) possessed by all living things.</term> conducted by a committee of the Medical Section of the Royal Academy of France. I felt that my only remaining task was to present this important document to my fellow countrymen, accompanied by an historical and explanatory introduction for those who had not...

<summary>The author explains that frequent inquiries from professionals pushed him to write this overview, as the subject is too complex for casual conversation. He notes that a friend provided him with a French Royal Academy report on animal magnetism, which he intends to present with a helpful introduction.</summary>
<keywords>animal magnetism, mesmerism, Royal Academy of France, medical report, scientific communication, preface</keywords>

->FIRST EDITION.<-

...hitherto paid any attention to the subject, to understand its details.*

This subject should be especially interesting to the medical profession, as well as to philosophers in general. If the vast variety of facts which have been gradually gathering during the last half-century can be considered satisfactorily proven, the force of the evidence in favor of *Animal Magnetism*—or by whatever other name we may choose to distinguish that peculiar type of sympathetic influence which has long been called so—becomes absolutely overwhelming <note>original: "irresistible"</note>. And if these facts are true, and not entirely imaginary <note>original: "supposititious"</note> and deceptive, it cannot be denied that they are destined <note>original: "calculated"</note> to open up many new and most important views in medical and physiological science—indeed, in the entire philosophy of the human mind.

Ever since the time of Paracelsus <note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a Swiss physician and alchemist who pioneered the use of minerals and chemicals in medicine but was also known for his eccentric and mystical theories.</note>—that strange mixture of genius and folly—physicians in general seem to have been in the habit of relying too exclusively on the effectiveness of chemical remedies, almost entirely neglecting many simple and natural, yet equally effective, healing <note>original: "sanative"</note> processes, especially those powerful mental <note>original: "psychical"</note> in—

***

<note>* This Report, as far as I am aware, has not been published in France. A specific number of copies, however, were lithographed <term>lithographed: A printing process using a stone or metal plate; here it implies a limited private distribution.</term> for the use of the members of the Academy; and the translation has been made from one of these.</note>

<summary>The author argues that the evidence for animal magnetism is becoming overwhelming and could revolutionize medical and psychological science. He critiques the medical profession's exclusive focus on chemical drugs since the time of Paracelsus, which he believes has led to the neglect of natural mental healing processes.</summary>

influences, which appear to have been known and employed in ancient times, and which are developed with such prodigious effect in magnetic treatment. Thus, for example, in cases of epilepsy and other spasmodic diseases, the regular practitioner would perhaps prescribe the internal administration of lunar caustic, ammoniate of copper, or some other dangerous drug; whereas, the magnetic doctor would cure the patient as speedily, as effectively, and probably more safely, by means of a few simple and apparently insignificant manipulations. This is a circumstance which surely deserves the serious attention of the profession; especially since, if it continues to be neglected by regular physicians, the treatment risks being unskillfully practiced and probably abused by unqualified practitioners <note>original: "empiric"</note>.*

The interesting and instructive works of Sprengel, Reil, Treviranus, Gmelin, Wienholt, Autenrieth, and many others, are known to only a few; and when any mention happens to be made of the subject of *Animal Magnetism*, it is at best received with ignorant ridicule, or with a haughty reference to the superseded report of the French Commissioners in 1784; as if nothing had been done since that period toward a more profound experimental investigation and improvement of magnetic treatment.

But it is evident that our physicians cannot long remain ignorant of these matters without falling greatly behind the times in respect to their professional knowledge. To them, therefore, I would respectfully, but earnestly, recommend a scientific and impartial inquiry into the subject. They are unquestionably the most competent to conduct the investigation, the most interested in its result, and the best qualified to make the discovery—provided they shall be ultimately satisfied that it really is a discovery—most beneficial to the interests of science and to the public welfare. In any case, they should no longer show total ignorance of a subject which has long been discussed in almost every physiological textbook on the Continent.

<header>PREFACE.</header>

Within the limits which I had prescribed for myself in this publication, it was found quite impossible to fully explain all the details of this interesting subject. This would have required, at the very least, a large volume. All that I intended for myself, therefore, at this time, was merely to give such an introductory notice of this discovery as might prepare the reader, to some degree, for a more serious study of its nature and principles, and of the evidence by which its reality is supported. Should the present minor publication attract any significant share of attention, additional information can easily be communicated in the future.

**Edinburgh,**
**15th April 1833.**

In attempting this difficult and very praiseworthy task, I may admire their boldness, but I cannot promise them success. Yet until they have done all this, they must not be allowed to boast of having refuted <term>Animal Magnetism</term>.

We are too prone to judge the reality of things by their more familiar external appearances, and, forgetting the first aphorism of Lord Bacon, to expect that Nature will always accommodate her operations to our preconceived notions of possibility, and adapt her phenomena to our arbitrary systems of philosophy. In a certain sense, indeed, universal nature may be said to constitute one grand and incomprehensible miracle of Divine Power. But do these miracles, which pervade all nature, cease to be miracles because they are common to all existence? They are still miracles, only subject to certain laws which are generally recognized. Hence, it happens that we only consider as a miracle whatever appears to us to deviate from these general laws and does not seem to coincide with other common phenomena. For instance, if the exalted psychical powers of some individuals—such as the *clairvoyance* of somnambulists—were a property common to all people in general, nobody would consider it miraculous, but rather as an endowment conferred by nature upon all mankind. However, exceptions and deviations from a general rule are disputed and denied unless they become as obvious to the senses as the influence of the magnet, which we recognize when it attracts iron, even though we do not comprehend its cause. I am merely about to lay before the public a class of very interesting natural facts which, although many of them have been occasionally observed for thousands of years, have until now been too much disregarded by philosophers, and, consequently, still await a satisfactory explanation. Should I have occasion to bring forward any theoretical or speculative notions upon this subject, it will only be for the purpose of showing the analogy that exists between these facts and other known phenomena of nature, or of showing how ingenious men have attempted to explain things which to many appear to be perfectly anomalous and inexplicable. I trust, however, that the intelligent reader will carefully distinguish between theory and fact, and beware of permitting the former to draw his attention away from the latter. In the second place, it has been urged as an objection against the practice of **Animal Magnetism** that it is uncertain in its operation. But it is illogical to conclude that, because the magnetic treatment does not invariably produce the desired effect, it is therefore altogether inoperative and useless. Certain unknown, perhaps accidental, circumstances may counteract its usual effectiveness in particular instances; indeed, several of these circumstances have already been discovered and made known, and others may be detected upon further experience. The same thing, however, it may be observed, sometimes occurs in ordinary medical practice. A thousand childless marriages take place; yet, based on the strength of this fact, no one would be foolish enough to deny that the multiplication of mankind is brought about by the union of the sexes. The subject itself is sufficiently curious and interesting, and worthy of the most serious investigation; and it is difficult to imagine how any class of men, claiming a love for scientific pursuits and possessing every opportunity for extending their knowledge in an important field, can look with coldness upon an overwhelming mass of accumulated evidence, which has already forced complete conviction upon the minds of thousands of the most learned and enlightened individuals in Europe, and promises to open up many new and most interesting views in the philosophy of man. [Spe]culation has been the besetting sin of all animal magnetists from the days of **MESMER** downward. If we are ever to have a just and adequate theory of animal magnetism, it must be made to comprehend not merely a few phenomena which may happen to have been developed in the practice of a single individual as a result of the employment of one particular process; but it must embrace a vast mass of facts which have been accumulating for centuries, although only recently subjected to scientific investigation. These phenomena, too, must be contemplated in all the varieties of their manifestation—in all the different phases in which they present themselves to the observation of the inquirer. It would be better, in the meantime, to have no theory at all, than one

are well known. But some individuals have been occasionally placed in a state of magnetic sleep and insensibility by a single glance from the eye of their magnetizer, and again recalled to life and sensibility by the same means.

It is rather curious that the unfavorable report of the French academicians in 1784 notices and actually admits the reality of these last-mentioned facts. In speaking of the magnetic patients, the report observes:

> "All are subject to the one who magnetizes them; however much they may be in an apparent slumber, his voice, a look, or a sign withdraws them from it. One cannot help but recognize in these constant effects a great power that agitates the patients and masters them, and of which the magnetizer seems to be the depository."

Metals, however, have been found to exercise a peculiar influence upon some constitutional idiosyncrasies, as well as upon magnetic patients. But we cannot base a correct and legitimate conclusion regarding the real cause of a phenomenon on the particular means that may happen to be used for producing it in some individual instances. Other causes may be in operation which we do not immediately perceive and, therefore, cannot appreciate.

The history of the science was brought down to the celebrated Report of the Committee of the Royal Academy of Medicine of Paris in 1831, which gave a fresh *impetus* to the investigation throughout Europe. It only remains for us to bring our historical sketch up to the present time.

It was hardly to be expected that the Report in question—cautious, moderate, able, and accurate as it was—should have altogether escaped the petty objections of some of those individuals who, for whatever reasons, had always shown an obstinate and irrational skeptical opposition toward the subject of investigation, and demonstrated a deep-seated jealousy of the introduction of the magnetic practice. Among these, **M. Dubois** of Amiens distinguished himself by his unreasonable violence and bitterness.* He published a fault-finding

---

<note>* The following anecdote may perhaps, in some measure, account for the violent hostility which **M. Dubois** has shown toward **Animal Magnetism**.

A patient had been suffering for eleven years from *fistula in ano* and stricture of the *rectum*. She had been placed under the treatment of a great number of the most eminent surgeons and physicians of France and had used the waters of Bagnères without success. # INTRODUCTION.
---
It is not uncommon for people who are ignorant of the nature of the alleged phenomena of **Animal Magnetism** to denounce them as pretended miracles and hold them up to ridicule. This is extremely irrational. A miracle is a violation of some general and known law of nature resulting from the immediate interposition of a Superior Power; and, in the sense of this definition, none of the philosophical adherents of the doctrine claim that there are any miracles in **Animal Magnetism**. The experiments, indeed, by which the reality of its peculiar phenomena has been established, have disclosed a number of extraordinary and most interesting facts; but the occasional occurrence of every fact, however uncommon, is capable of being demonstrated by evidence. It can be shown to be the result of natural causes, and it then becomes quite unphilosophical to regard it as a real or pretended miracle.

Indeed, this spirit of hostility has been carried so far that individuals claiming to have made discoveries in this department of science might consider themselves fortunate if, along with the belittling of their pursuits and the ridicule of their alleged facts, they were not also denounced and persecuted as worthless or even harmful impostors. The instinct of animals is formed by this sense, and it enables them to foresee dangers which are near. It resides in the bones, the bowels, the ganglion, and the plexus of the nerves. To answer such fantasies would be a mere waste of time."

This is all, so far as I have observed, that M. Magendie has condescended to say about animal magnetism—a ridiculously incomplete allusion to one of those hundred theories which have been put forth with a view to account for a certain class of phenomena. On the subject of the phenomena themselves, he is quite silent. Now, I would just take the liberty of asking M. Magendie in what part of the writings of Bacon he has found a single passage which, either directly or by implication, can warrant us in excluding from philosophy the consideration of any class of facts which have been established by incontrovertible evidence, and of the reality of which every intelligent man may satisfy himself through experiment and observation? Lord Bacon was not quite such a blockhead as some of his so-called disciples would make him out to be.

In one of his notes to the work of M. Magendie, Dr. Milligan observes that "*sleepwalkers* afford a most perplexing object of study." Now, surely that labor is not useless, and that time is not misspent, which is occupied in attempting to unravel this perplexity in the true spirit of the Baconian philosophy by collecting and classifying the facts.

## CHAPTER I.

The name of *Animal Magnetism* has been given to that organic susceptibility which renders the nervous system of one individual capable of being affected, in various ways, by particular processes performed by another, especially when accompanied by faith, or, at least, a certain surrender in the patient, and by an energetic effort of will on the part of the operator. The same name is also used to designate the processes themselves, through which the desired effects are sought to be produced.<note>The name, *Animal Magnetism*, has been considered improper by many because it conveys no adequate idea of the nature and extent of the subject; and also because it seems to imply a questionable theory. This latter objection, indeed, has evidently misled many ingenious but superficial inquirers, who</note>

But the name that Mesmer was originally led to give to his discovery, because of certain circumstances that will be explained hereafter, could not now be changed without considerable inconvenience; nor is it, perhaps, desirable that it should be. Several of the sciences, it may be observed, have long since outgrown the names by which they were first designated: As one instance among many, the science of *electricity* was originally named after a Greek word meaning *amber*. Whether the phenomena produced during the processes practiced by Mesmer and his disciples have anything in them similar to magnetism remains a debatable point to this day. The majority of practical magnetizers are decidedly of the opinion that such an analogy does exist. But, really, this is a matter of relatively little importance. It is much easier to classify these phenomena than to give an appropriate and entirely unobjectionable name to that department of science under which they are to be arranged, especially as long as their cause is obscure or ambiguous. It is of more importance to science, however, to collect and classify facts than to quibble about names.

number of the observations and experiments which have been made, and the similarity of the phenomena which have been observed to occur in similar circumstances.

2. To satisfy ourselves with respect to the general character, intellectual fitness, and resulting credibility of the witnesses.

3. To scrutinize the circumstances in which the various experiments were conducted, with a view to detecting any possible sources of error.

4. To be assured of the precision and clarity of the facts themselves, of their dependence upon the same principle, and of the rational impossibility of attributing them to more than a single cause; and,

5. If possible, to repeat for our own satisfaction—or cause to be repeated in our presence by others—the experiments by which the phenomena have been produced, and to do so in the same circumstances and under the same conditions. *

Do not our most eminent professors occasionally fail to produce the expected result?</note>

By judiciously following these rules, every intelligent and candid inquirer may succeed in obtaining complete conviction; whereas, he who refuses to inquire is not entitled to decide.

In proceeding to carry out the task I have undertaken in the present publication, however, I am well aware that I may expose myself, in the eyes of some individuals, to the charge of drawing heavily upon the credulity of my countrymen. For such a charge, indeed, I am fully prepared, and do not avoid it; but, fortunately, I may share the burden with a numerous host of individuals of far higher achievements and scientific reputation than any to which I can claim; while I may hope to find the weight diminish, in proportion as knowledge extends. My sole object is to ascertain the truth in an important subject of inquiry; and this can only be done by an examination of the evidence applicable to the different points of the case. And here I may take the opportunity of declaring, that I shall bring forward no facts, as such, unless they are sufficiently attested by men of unimpeachable veracity;—men abundantly qualified by their scientific habits and achievements, by their perceptiveness and cautious spirit of research, for investigating the reality of the circumstances which they profess to have witnessed;—and who, besides, could have no motive for deception, no conceivable inte-

<margin>
* "In every scientific investigation, it must be kept in mind that efficient causes are beyond our reach. The objects of our research are physical causes only, by which we mean nothing more than the uniform sequences of events, as confirmed by extensive observation. What we call the explanation of phenomena consists in being able to trace distinctly all the links of such a chain of sequences, so as to perceive their uniform relation to each other. Thus, there may be many instances in which we are acquainted with facts forming part of such a chain and are satisfied that they are so connected, while we cannot explain their connection. This is caused by the lack of some fact which forms an intermediate part of the chain, the discovery of which would enable us to see the relation of the whole sequence—or, in common language, to explain the phenomena. Such a chain of facts was, at one time, presented by the rise of water in a vacuum to the height of thirty-two feet. The circumstances were well known, as was their uniform relation; that is to say, the fact of a vacuum, the fact of the water rising, and the fact of this uniformly taking place. But the phenomenon could not be explained, for an intermediate fact was required to show the manner in which these known facts were connected. The doctrine of nature abhorring a vacuum afforded no explanation, for it furnished no fact; but the fact required was supplied by the discoveries of Torricelli on atmospheric pressure. The chain of events was then filled up, or, in common language, the phenomenon was accounted for.

"There are, indeed, many cases in which the investigation of intermediate events in the chain of sequences is beyond our reach. In these, we must be satisfied with a knowledge of the facts and their actual connection as we observe them, without being able to trace the events on which the connection depends. This happens in some of the great phenomena of Nature, such as gravitation and magnetism. We know the facts, but we can—

I may here observe that the most eminent philosophers—those who have made the most profound researches into the laws and operations of Nature—are generally the most inclined to speak with appropriate modesty about facts that they themselves have had no opportunity to investigate, and which they can only judge based on the evidence of others and from known analogies. To prove this, I may refer to the following remarks by the most illustrious disciple of Newton, which are particularly applicable to the present occasion. The celebrated M. de Laplace, in his *Essai sur les Probabilités*, observes that "of all the instruments we can employ to enable us to discover the imperceptible agents of nature, the nerves are the most sensitive, especially when their sensitivity is heightened by particular causes. It is by means of them that we have discovered the slight electricity developed by two heterogeneous metals. The singular phenomena resulting from the extreme sensitivity of the nerves in some individuals have given rise to various opinions regarding the existence of a new agent, which has been called *Animal Magnetism*, to the action of common magnetism, and to the influence of the

---

<note>...not account for them; that is, we are ignorant of certain intermediate facts by which those we do know are connected together."—**ABERCROMBIE**, *Inquiries concerning the Intellectual Powers*, 4th edition, pp. 413—415.</note>

> sun and moon in some nervous affections, and, lastly, to the impressions which may be experienced from the proximity of metals, or of running water. It is natural to suppose that the action of these causes is very feeble, and that it may be easily disturbed by accidental circumstances; but because in some cases it has not been manifested at all, we are not entitled to conclude that it does not exist. We are so far from being acquainted with all the agents of nature, and their different modes of action, that it would be quite unphilosophical to deny the existence of the phenomena merely because they are inexplicable in the present state of our knowledge. It is our duty, however, to examine them with an attention all the more scrupulous in proportion to how difficult we find it to admit them; and it is here that the calculation of probabilities becomes indispensable, in order to determine to what degree we ought to multiply our observations and experiments, with a view to obtain, in favor of the agents which they seem to indicate, a probability superior to the reasons we may have for rejecting them."

# ANIMAL MAGNETISM. 74

*Anatomie Comparée*, expressed his opinion regarding Animal Magnetism in the following terms:

> "I must confess that it is very difficult to distinguish the effect of the patient's imagination from the physical effect produced by the operator. However, the effects produced upon persons already unconscious before the start of the operation, those that occur in others after the operation has deprived them of sensation, and those manifested by animals, do not allow us to doubt that the proximity of two living bodies, in certain positions and with certain motions, has a real effect, independent of any influence from the imagination of either one. It also seems clear enough that these effects are due to some kind of communication established between their nervous systems."

I shall have occasion later to refer to the opinions expressed upon this subject by the late Professor Dugald Stewart, and by other eminent philosophers and physicians. In the meantime, I may observe that the preceding examples of philosophical judgment present a striking contrast to the arrogant, insincere, and irrational methods by which most opponents of Animal Magnetism have attempted to discredit the discoveries of the professors of that doc-

"**The essential point,**" says Nicole, following Aristotle, "**when any question arises regarding facts that are extraordinary and difficult to understand, is not to demonstrate how they exist, but to prove that they do exist.**"* "**We must not decide,**" says Father Lebrun, "**that a thing is impossible because of the common belief that it cannot exist; for the opinion of man cannot set limits to the operations of nature, or to the power of the Almighty.**"†

There is no doubt that, when phenomena of an extraordinary character are presented to us for the first time, to which we can perceive nothing ana-

> deception, *plus* some chance and accidental coincidence, might determine the direction in which skepticism should vibrate. For nine years, the subject of <term>Zoo-Magnetism</term> has been before me. I have traced it historically, collected a mass of documents in French, German, Italian, and the Latinists of the sixteenth century, and have never neglected an opportunity of questioning eyewitnesses—for example, Tieck, Treviranus, De Prati, Meyer, and others of literary or medical celebrity—and I remain where I was, and where the first reading of Kluge’s work had left me, without having moved an inch backward or forward. The reply of Treviranus, the famous botanist, to me when he was in London, is worth recording:—"*Ich habe gesehen was (Ich weiss das) Ich nicht würde geglaubt haben auf ihren Erzählung, etc.*"—'I have seen what I am certain I would not have believed on your telling; and in all reason, therefore, I can neither expect nor wish that you should believe on mine.'"—**COLERIDGE**; *Table-Talk*, vol. i. pp. 107, etc.

* <note>“In the acquisition of facts, we depend partly upon our own observation and partly on the testimony of others. In the degree of evidence which we require for new facts, we are also influenced, as was formerly stated, by their probability or their accordance with facts previously known to us; and, for facts which appear to us improbable, we require a higher amount of testimony than for those in accordance with our previous knowledge. This necessary caution, however, while it preserves us from credulity, should not, on the other hand, be allowed to engender skepticism; for both these extremes are equally unworthy of a mind which devotes itself with candor to the discovery of truth.”</note>—**ABERCROMBIE**; *Inquiries concerning the Intellectual Powers*, p. 378.

## CHAPTER II.

The effects which are alleged to have been produced through the influence of that agent which has been named <term>Animal Magnetism</term>, appear to have so far excited little sensation in this country, except as an occasional subject of ridicule. In the case of people who have never made any serious inquiry into the subject, the very extraordinary, and apparently mysterious and unaccountable, character of the facts—so startling at first glance—might almost justify the derision with which they always seem inclined to treat them. But anyone who once enters into a sober investigation of these facts, and becomes, to some extent, aware of their number, their universality, the conditions under which they occur, their similarity to each other, and the overwhelming evidence which exists in favor of their reality, must soon perceive that they deserve more serious attention. There are various simple operations in almost constant practice among mankind, performed instinctively, as it were, which—due to their very frequency and apparent insignificance—scarcely engage our attention and consequently give rise to no reflection. We find, indeed, a number of floating opinions regarding the object and efficacy of some of these seemingly trifling operations, which have been transmitted from age to age, until they have at length been permitted to settle down and mingle with the elements of popular belief. However, educated and scientific men, especially in this age of intellect, have generally agreed to regard all such practices with indifference and to reject all such opinions with contempt as the product of mere ignorance and prejudice. those habits of thinking, those instinctive principles and feelings, which Nature herself, for the wisest of purposes no doubt, seems to have originally implanted in the minds even of the most primitive of mankind. Adherents of magnetism do not admit that there is much, if any, analogy between this mode of cure and magnetic processes. I would not have considered it proper, however, to have omitted all notice of the belief and corresponding practices alluded to; the more especially as, notwithstanding all the facts which have been brought forward, and the theories which have been proposed upon the subject, we are still admittedly very ignorant of the true causes which operate in producing the phenomena of Animal Magnetism; and it has never yet been correctly determined to what extent these phenomena may depend upon the physical means employed, or upon the psychical influences which are exerted, or developed, during the treatment. The general, almost universal, prevalence of the popular belief respecting the existence of the influence in question, appeared to be a circumstance of too much importance to be passed over entirely without notice.*

> "A member of the Academy of Sciences declared to me that he knew a lady who was long afflicted with heart palpitations. She was advised to wear on her breast a hazelnut, hollowed out, and then filled with mercury, and well-sealed. As soon as she began to wear this amulet, the palpitations ceased. After a few days she thought herself cured, and laid aside the amulet. The palpitations returned; and the same thing took place during several years."

Some writers on Animal Magnetism have been led to attribute a great deal of influence to the human eye; and in this opinion, they also seem to be supported by a very ancient and generally prevalent popular belief, which, in many instances, no doubt, may have degenerated into superstition. This belief, however, seems to have existed from the earliest times. Pliny informs us, in his *Natural History*, that a particular eye color and a double pupil (probably meaning a multicolored or spotted *iris*) were believed to indicate that the people with this eye color or structure were uniquely endowed with this kind of magnetic power.*

Of all the bodily organs, none can be considered as much an immediate and faithful interpreter of internal thoughts, feelings, and emotions as the eye. I remember reading in a newspaper some years ago an account of the escape of a tiger from confinement, which caused great terror and confusion in the streets of London. A gentleman, happening to come suddenly out of a house without any previous knowledge or suspicion of his danger, found the animal crouched within a few yards of him. Fortunately, this gentleman had spent some part of his life in the East Indies and was acquainted with the nature of these ferocious animals. Instead of attempting to make his escape, he stood perfectly still and fixed his eyes steadily upon the tiger, who, in the course of a few seconds, made a bound to the opposite side of the street and soon left the gentleman in complete security.

There are also various other sympathies, although they are of less importance regarding our usual faculties in the waking state and in relation to external life.

In the solar *plexus*, which some of the ancients called the *cerebrum abdominale*, the soul is thought to derive the materials necessary for forming its intuitive judgments.

A number of eminent German and French anatomists and physiologists in recent times have devoted much effort to investigating the structure and path of the nervous *ganglia* and *plexus*, and of the various abdominal nerves connected with them. (See **J. F. MECKEL**; *De vera nervi intercostalis origine*. *In diss. de quinto pari nervorum cerebri*. Goeting. 1784.—**J. G. WALTER**; *Tabulae nervorum thoracis et abdominis*. Berolini, 1783.) Bichat in France and Hufeland in Germany developed the idea, at about the same time, that all these nerves—though organically connected with the cerebral nerves—formed a unique and independent system of nervous influence. (See Bichat's *General Anatomy*, and C. W. Hufeland's *Pathologie*.) This idea was subsequently pursued further and explained with great clarity and ingenuity by Autenrieth (*Handbuch der Physiologie*), Burdach (*Physiologie*), and especially by Reil (*On the peculiar properties of the Ganglionic System, and its relation to the Cerebral System*; in the *Archiv für Physiologie*, vol. vii. No. 2, pp. 189–254). Humboldt (in the *Gazette Litteraire de Berlin*, 1788, p. 312) afterwards extended this theory with his evidence in favor of the external expansion of nervous influence.

As it would take me too far afield to enter minutely into the details of this ingenious theory, I believe it is enough for me to have pointed out the various works in which it is explained and to recommend further investigation by competent researchers. I may observe, however, that the theory is of great importance to Animal Magnetism; as most magnetic phenomena seem explainable only by the relationship between the cerebral and ganglionic systems.

Whether these sympathetic actions originate from a connection between the different nerves, which are the sole instruments of all sensations; or whether they are determined by mental sensations, as maintained by Dr. Alison—these are questions which I willingly leave to be decided by scientific physiologists and physicians.

## CHAPTER V.

Hippocrates long ago affirmed that Nature herself frequently cured diseases; he believed that her most vigilant attendants and observers were the best physicians. This observation has since been repeated often, and the opinion appears to have given rise to various hypotheses concerning the nature of this healing principle. <note>“There is no curable malady from which the patient does not sometimes recover—without the aid of external remedies—through the unassisted efforts of the vital principle. *All the more* should this cure occur when, by means of a methodical and well-understood transmission of an effective fluid, the patient’s defective fluid is restored and better directed in its action. And let it not be thought that it is primarily the quantity or the quality of drugs that effects cures; Nature alone cures by restoring—whether by natural or artificial means—order to disturbed functions. A cure is nothing more than a victory obtained by the vital principle over the opposing forces presented by the disease.”—*Memoir on the Vital Fluid, etc., by Dr. Ch. in the Library of Animal Magnetism, vol. ii. p. 26.*</note>

These opinions are supported, in part, by the experience of the celebrated Dr. Hoffmann and by the great success in recent times of the homeopathic system of medicine, which has proved to be such a <term>shibboleth</term> for the profession.

Even in an ordinary state, we can relieve ourselves from pain and suffering by a firm exercise of will—by fixing our attention upon other objects; indeed, very serious complaints may occasionally be cured in this way. How, then, can it be denied that a profound devotional feeling, which in some individuals far surpasses all other feelings in power and intensity, may likewise have the greatest influence upon the human body?

Indeed, it would be far more incomprehensible if this were not the case than it is that it actually happens; and it must appear at least as incomprehensible that wine, which exhilarates and to a certain degree elevates the human soul, should also be an excellent medicine in many diseases, as it is that a firm confidence in God should penetrate both body and soul and restore their failing energies.

No true physician, therefore, will be surprised when people are relieved from physical suffering by a strong and lively faith; and he will readily allow the less informed to represent these cures as miracles, while he sees in them only the effects of the same universal power of nature—of the same Spirit—which lies at the base of all other phenomena. These so-called miraculous cures must interest him even as mere natural phenomena, since from them he can derive new proofs of the great importance of *medicina psychica* (psychological medicine), and he will be just as edified in his own way by these facts as the devout mind which views them as miracles.

> "Since my arrival about a year ago, I have witnessed the successive death of about four-fifths of those who have arrived from Europe. > ...to believe, on slight grounds, events that are almost always exaggerated by enthusiasm; but instead of feeling annoyed when similar accounts are published, philosophers would do well to investigate and ascertain the facts, to present them in their proper degree of importance, and to enlighten the public on the subject of their nature and causes. I am much mistaken if such conduct would not make a greater impression than a ridiculous exasperation or stale mockery, which are more calculated to excite fanaticism than to destroy it. It is time that science should frankly take possession of these miraculous cures, which are so evidently within its domain and which constitute a very interesting chapter of that powerful influence of the mental over the physical nature of man—an influence so frequently appealed to, and yet until now so little appreciated in its more curious results."—*Le Globe, as cited above.*

> “We all know that, in undertaking any difficult task which requires moral energy, the confidence we have in our powers and the hope of success contribute much toward enabling us to surmount obstacles. When one body of troops marches to attack another, if it is well convinced of its superiority—if it has no doubt of obtaining the victory—it will possess a prodigious advantage over the enemy, even although the latter should be superior in numbers. When soldiers make an assault, we see them scale walls and clear ditches which would certainly have stopped them if they were not previously convinced that nothing could resist their impetuosity. Magnetism has for its principle a moral action; it is the will which darts forth the fluid as it impresses motion; and is it surprising that confidence should increase its energy?”—DELEUZE; *Defense du Magnetisme Animal*, p. 106.

### CHAPTER VI.

AFTER the preceding episode—which I trust was not entirely unnecessary, uninteresting, or uninstructive—regarding those sympathetic and moral influences that are sometimes active in curing diseases, and which, if treated with the detail their importance deserves, would probably take up far too large a part of this publication; I shall now move on to a much more extraordinary topic. I will direct my readers' attention to some very remarkable recorded instances of the wonderful power of human volition: first over the physical body of the individual exercising it, and then over the bodies of others.

Indeed, the most surprising cures are said to have been occasionally achieved mentally—and, as it were, magically—without using any tangible or measurable remedy, or any visible medium, through the mere influence of an individual's will and determination over their physical organs. **Joannes Bohnius**, * etc. All of these writers, and many others, assumed the existence of a universal magnetic power by which they attempted to explain the interdependence and reciprocal action of bodies in general, and the phenomena of vital organization in particular. They also broadly and distinctly maintained the proposition that the human will or imagination, when energetically activated, is capable of producing certain perceptible effects upon the organisms of other living beings, even at a considerable distance.

This last proposition has perhaps been most clearly articulated by Pomponatius and Van Helmont. Considering them as the representatives of this entire class of writers, I think it is sufficient to give a summary of the opinions they held regarding the subject we are now investigating.

Although the time in which this is done cannot be measured, it must certainly happen within twenty-four hours; and I know how to do this, and have done it quite often. The late Abbot Trithemius also knew and performed the same thing.*”—*On Occult Philosophy*, book 3.

On the ***Magnetic Cure of Wounds***, is, in this respect, particularly remarkable. It was intended as an answer to two authors who had written upon the same subject—Goclenius, a physical philosopher then in considerable repute, and Father Robert, a Jesuit. The first had maintained the reality of the cures effected by magnetic means and ascribed them to natural causes. The latter did not deny these cures but condemned them as proceeding from the devil.

Van Helmont shows that Goclenius had feebly defended the cause of truth; and he proves, in opposition to Father Robert, that there is nothing criminal or diabolical in the magnetic treatment, but that all the phenomena depend upon natural causes. "**Magnetism**," says he, "is a universal agent; there is nothing new in it but the name; and it is a paradox only to those who are disposed to ridicule everything, and who ascribe to the influence of Satan all those phenomena which they cannot explain."<note>Magnetism, because it flourishes everywhere, contains nothing new besides the name; nor is it a paradox except to those who ridicule all things, and relegate to the domain of Satan whatever they do not understand.</note> He defines **Magnetism** to be "that occult influence which bodies exert over each other at a distance, whether by attraction or by impulsion."<note>So we call that occult adjustment by which something absent in...</note> The medium or vehicle of this influence,

There is nothing more striking, and probably to most people at first glance, more incomprehensible in the works of Van Helmont—and indeed in those of most of the early writers on the subject of Magnetism—than the vast and mysterious influence which they ascribe to the power of energetic and concentrated volition; an opinion which could hardly be based on anything but experience of the fact. In this respect, too, there appears to be a remarkable coincidence between their opinions and the doctrines and practice of the Magnetic School of Barbarin, which the reader will find explained in the following sections.

The will, according to Van Helmont, is the first of powers. It was by the will of the Almighty that the universe was created; it was by volition that motion was originally impressed upon all objects; it is the will existing in man which is the principle of all his actions. Volition belongs to all spiritual beings; it is more active and powerful in them in proportion as they are disengaged from matter; and the energy with which it operates without the assistance of bodily organs is the essential characteristic of pure spirits. It would be premature, perhaps, at present to give any account of the observations and experiments of Van Helmont on the subject of the ecstatic, or magnetic, crisis. In the meantime, I may observe that it appears quite evident from the entire works of this author that he was not only perfectly well acquainted with magnetic influence, but that he made use of it professionally and placed great confidence in its effects. He himself, indeed, informs us that when the plague was raging in the town of Brussels, he thought it his duty to seize the opportunity to educate himself and to be useful to others. He accordingly offered his services to attend the sick; neither fatigue nor the fear of infection could abate his zeal or extinguish his charity. 

> "Perceiving," he says, "that most of the physicians deserted the sick, I devoted myself to their service, and God preserved me from the contagion. All, when they saw me, seemed to be refreshed with hope and joy; while I, supported by faith and confidence, persuaded myself that God would at length confer upon me the science of an adept."*

* Dr. Bertrand mentions two very curious facts, falling within his own experience, which seem to prove that somnambulists are capable of penetrating the thoughts of others with whom they are placed *en rapport*. In performing upon his first somnambulist the process by which he was accustomed to awaken her, while having a firm determination at the same time that she should not awake, she was instantly seized with violent convulsions. On his inquiring what was the matter, she answered, “How! You bid me awake, and yet you don't wish me to awake.”

The other example is the following: A poor woman, uneducated and unable to read, was said to be capable, in somnambulism, of understanding the meaning of words of whose significance she was ignorant when awake; and, in fact, she explained to Dr. Bertrand, in the most exact and ingenious manner, what we ought to understand by the word *encephalon*, which he proposed to her; a phenomenon which, unless we assume the hypothesis of a coincidence as difficult to admit as the supposed faculty itself, can only be explained by acknowledging that this woman read, in the very thoughts of the doctor, the meaning of the word about which she was questioned.

This fact of the intimate *rapport* existing between the operator and the patient may afford us a key to many of the mysteries of Animal Magnetism; but it is nonetheless extraordinary in itself.—**Bertrand**, p. 439.

Such is the story told by Glanvill, an author perfectly worthy of all credit, who afterward maintains that this strange power of the imagination—

> “I once told a man, who was curious and conceited enough about such matters, that I saw a kind of juggler who had a deck of cards and could tell a man what card he was thinking of. This supposedly learned man told me I was mistaken; ‘for,’ said he, ‘it was not the knowledge of the man’s thought—for that belongs only to God—but it was the *enforcing of a thought upon him, and binding his imagination with a stronger one*, so that he could think of no other card.’ And then he asked me a question or two, which I thought he did only craftily, knowing beforehand what the juggler’s tricks used to be. ‘Sir,’ said he, ‘do you remember whether he named the card the man thought of himself, or told another person to name it?’ I answered, truthfully, that he told another to name it. To which he said, ‘Just as I thought; for,’ said he, ‘he himself could not have exerted such a strong imagination; but by telling the other person the card—who believed that the juggler was an extraordinary man and could do strange things—that other man caught a strong imagination.’ I listened to him, thinking that, despite his vanity, he spoke cleverly. Then he asked me another question. He said, ‘Do you remember whether he told the man to think of the card first, and afterward whispered in the other man’s ear what he should say; or else, did he whisper first in the ear of the man who was to name the card, saying that such a man would think of such a card, and afterward told the man to think of a card?’ I told him, as was true, that he first whispered in the man’s ear that such a person would think of such a card. At this, the learned man greatly rejoiced and was pleased with himself, saying, ‘Look, you can see that my opinion is right; for if the man had thought first, his thought would have been fixed; but because the other person imagined it first, he bound the man’s thoughts.’ Although this stayed with me somewhat, I made light of it and said I thought it was a conspiracy between the juggler and the two servants—though, indeed, I had no reason to think so, for they were both my father’s servants, and he had never performed in the house before.”

### CHAPTER VII.

**THERE** are some persons whose minds are so skeptically constituted that they find great difficulty in bringing themselves to believe any uncommon fact, or series of facts, however incontrovertibly established by evidence, unless they are also in a position to give a rational and apparently satisfactory explanation of the principles upon which those facts depend. Such persons generally remain skeptics regarding both religion and philosophy. But the explanation required by these individuals is by no means essential to our conviction of the reality of any phenomenon, nor, in many cases, can it be easily provided. Facts are believed every day based upon observation, or upon testimony, which we would be exceedingly puzzled to account for if called upon to do so. In the Introduction to this work, I have shown that there are facts which had been observed for thousands of years before even their existence was generally admitted. A common proverb tells us that "there is nothing new but what has been forgotten."

Indeed, skepticism in this matter is now limited entirely to those people who stubbornly refuse to investigate.

## It is but fair to observe, however, that there is a variety of other magnetic phenomena—and these

<note>along with the changes produced in inanimate bodies by apparently trivial and inadequate causes, should lead those who stubbornly deny the possibility of the facts of Animal Magnetism—which are, perhaps, the effects of similar causes on the living organism—to investigate their reality before dismissing them.</note> To all such people, I would like to submit the following observations.

Placing two different metals on top of one another produces Galvanism. The friction of a glass plate generates Electricity. M. Haüy discovered that the simple pressure of a hand upon a tourmaline made it electrical. The point of contact gives attraction all its force. Iron attaches itself to a magnet at the point of contact and becomes magnetic itself through friction; it follows the direction of the magnet from a distance, even through intervening solid objects. Touch develops <term>caloric</term>. Friction causes carriage wheels to catch fire. Phosphorus emits light as a result of friction. Chemistry teaches us that friction causes surprising explosions. The combination of hydrogen with an elementary substance called *cyanogen* produces *hydrocyanic acid*. This acid, more commonly called *Prussic acid*, possesses very unusual physical properties. It freezes at 15° and begins to boil at 26°—an interval so short that, if a single drop is exposed to the air, the evaporation of one part produces enough cold to freeze the rest. In its pure state, this acid is a most deadly poison. The smallest drop placed on an animal's tongue kills it as quickly as a bullet or a thunderbolt. The same substance that produces this terrifying poison when combined with hydrogen creates fulminating powders when united with oxygen.

Iron filings, immersed in a liquid as cold as the metal itself, instantly produce a violent boiling and flammable vapors. Indeed, this metal, solid as it is, is afterward somewhat broken down by that fluid and combines with it in such a way that it passes with the fluid through the finest filter.

## CHAPTER VIII.

In all ages and among all nations, phenomena similar to those now known to be produced by Animal Magnetism have been observed occasionally. Ancient writers, indeed, are full of allusions which, when carefully examined, leave no room for doubt that some knowledge of these processes—probably—and certainly of these susceptibilities, existed in early times. At a later period, indeed, the reality of these facts was either entirely denied, or the singular effects in question were attributed to imagination and delusion, or to the deceptions of the priesthood, aided by the ignorance and gullibility of the people. Elizabeth Bryant, aged 50, along with her two daughters, Elizabeth, aged 22, and Jane, aged 15, were charged with maliciously assaulting an old woman, Ann Burgess, a reputed witch, under the following circumstances: It appears that Elizabeth Bryant the younger had been suffering from fits, which were supposed to have been caused by the influence of some malignant spirit; consequently, the mother sought advice from a well-known sorcerer in the neighborhood. To break the charm, the conjurer gave her an amulet to protect the wearer against witchcraft, prescribed some medicines to be taken internally, and also provided a packet of herbs to be burned with specific ceremonies and incantations. But this was not all; for the prisoners actually believed the horrible idea that, to effectively dispel the charm, it was necessary to draw blood from the witch. Accordingly, having decided that the prosecutrix was the individual who had bewitched the young woman, they took the opportunity to assault her and draw blood from her arm by lacerating it dreadfully with a large nail. The prisoners were convicted and sentenced to imprisonment.

This trial is curious, as it provides an instance of the crude belief in witchcraft that, it would appear, is still prevalent in some remote parts of the country.

# CHAPTER IX.

ABOUT the middle of the seventeenth century, there appeared in England a certain gardener named Levret, an Irish gentleman named Valentine Greatrakes, and the notorious Dr. Streper, who cured, or pretended to cure, various diseases by stroking with the hand. Their activities caused a significant sensation at the time; but men of science of that period seem to have made no attempt to determine the exact facts or to investigate the subject physiologically. On the contrary, the effects of their treatment soon came to be regarded by some as a mere piece of trickery, and by others as the consequence of a unique power specifically bestowed by Nature upon these individuals.*

<note>* The learned Pechlinus, in his work titled *Observationum Physico-Medicarum libri tres*, Hamburg, 1691, has preserved a fairly thorough account of Greatrakes; and there is also an existing treatise said to have been written and published by that remarkable individual himself, titled *A Brief Account of Mr. Valentine Greatrakes, etc.*, London, 1666.</note>

The effectiveness of the treatment adopted by Greatrakes is at-

# ANIMAL MAGNETISM.

The method of Greatrakes consisted of applying his hands to the diseased parts and rubbing gently downwards. This is very similar to the most common and simplest process adopted by current magnetizers; and it is remarkable that the effects produced by this treatment appear to have borne a striking analogy to some of the most ordinary phenomena of Animal Magnetism: namely, increased excitement, different kinds of excretions, <term>alvine evacuations</term>, vomiting, etc. No mention, however, is made of sleep or somnambulism in the accounts given of the cures performed by Greatrakes; whether it was that he did not produce these phenomena, or that he did not particularly observe them. Indeed, it is remarked by Deleuze and by other writers on Animal Magnetism that somnambulism rarely appears when it is not sought to be excited, and that it may take place without being observed, as actually occurred to some of the early disciples of Mesmer.

Many interesting particulars relative to Greatrakes have been related by Joseph Glanvill—at

The philosophic Cudworth was among his patients and had firm faith in the efficacy of his treatment.

A mere denial cannot invalidate the facts so strongly attested, and the evidence is far beyond the reach of sophistry <note>fallacious reasoning</note>.*

A great many years later, there appeared a still more extraordinary character in the person of the German exorcist, John Joseph Gassner. Gassner was born in 1727 at Bratz, near Pludenz, in Suabia, and became a Catholic minister at Clösterle, in the bishopric of Chur. Having taken up the notion that most diseases arose from demoniacal possession and could be cured by exorcism, he began by curing some of his parishioners

monks and friars concerning things done in monasteries and private cells: An infinite number of the nobility, gentry, and clergy of Warwickshire and Worcestershire—persons too knowledgeable to be deceived, and too honorable and worthy to deceive—will testify that they have seen him publicly cure the lame, the blind, the deaf, and those perhaps not unfairly supposed to be demoniacs and lepers; besides asthma, epilepsy <note>falling sickness</note>, convulsion fits, hysteria <note>fits of the mother</note>, and old aches and pains.” After relating some of his own observations on the cases he had witnessed, Dr. Stubbe proceeds: “I considered that there was no manner of fraud in the performances, that his hands had no manner of medicines <note>medicaments</note> upon them, . . . . . . . . nor was his stroking so violent that much could be attributed to the friction. I observed that he used no manner of charms or unlawful words; sometimes he uttered a short prayer before he cured anyone, and always, after he had finished, he told them to give God the praise.” Now, where is the imposture in all this?

I find from the *Life of Flamsteed*, recently published, that the celebrated astronomer had also been a patient of Greatrakes; and although he does not seem to have derived much benefit from the treatment himself, yet he, too, bears ample testimony to the reality of the cures performed upon others, and to the general efficacy of the processes. Clergymen, physicians, and philosophers, therefore—and those contemporaries and eyewitnesses—all unite in giving the most unequivocal evidence in favor of Greatrakes.

There was also another natural magnetizer in Germany, in recent times, named Grabe, a groom, I believe, by profession, of whom I have read some published accounts. He appears to have possessed great powers of curing diseases by manipulation, and was very tireless and selfless in exercising them. Although a man of perfectly good character and active benevolence, his proceedings gave great offense to the Faculty, at whose request he suffered continual persecution. <note>Nothing can be more absurd and disgraceful than such persecution. When facts are supported by evidence, it is surely more rational to examine them philosophically than to attempt to invalidate them by discreditable means. False statements of facts can never gain any permanent credit; but when such statements are opposed, not by reason, but by ridicule and persecution, a considerable bias in their favor is naturally generated in the minds of all sober, serious, and disinterested inquirers. No doctrine, probably, was ever thoroughly eradicated by the persecution of its followers.</note>

At the same time, he was patronized by some medical men and other respectable individuals, who bore ample and satisfactory testimony to the propriety of his conduct and the effectiveness of his treatment.

### CHAPTER X.

FREDERICK ANTHONY MESMER, a native of Switzerland, was born on May 23, 1734. In his youth, he came to Vienna in very needy circumstances for the purpose of studying medicine; and after having attended the lectures of Van Swieten and De Haen for several years and taken his degree of Doctor of Medicine, he settled in that capital as a practicing physician and placed himself in a position of independence through an advantageous marriage. From his youth onward, he is said to have manifested a decided bias toward the uncommon and the marvelous; and his favorite employment was to search for the almost forgotten works of the old mystical writers, particularly those which treated of astrology, which he studied with great attention and earnestness. The consequence of this was that, upon the occasion of his promotion in the year 1766, he wrote and publicly defended an inaugural dissertation *On the Influence of the Planets upon the Human Body.* This treatise drew down upon him the almost universal .

The history of Perkinism, however, and its alleged refutation by Dr. Haygarth, provides strong supporting evidence—if any were needed—to confirm the reality of Animal Magnetism.

Perkins invented specific instruments called *Metallic Tractors*. Even his enemies admit that with these, he frequently relieved pain and performed remarkable cures. To disprove Perkinism, Dr. Haygarth created *wooden tractors*, with which he and others produced similar effects; indeed, these effects were allegedly even greater and more wonderful than those reported for Perkins’s patented *metallic tractors*. Therefore, Perkins’s patented tractors were a piece of quackery. This is true—and so were Dr. Haygarth’s *wooden tractors*. Physicians may cry "quackery" as loudly and as often as they wish, but they will never succeed in eliminating this annoying deception, in one form or another, until they condescend—like their colleagues on the Continent—to conduct a philosophical investigation into the principles and methods of Mesmer and his followers.

The effects of Perkinism, as well as those of Animal Magnetism, were attributed by all *learned* physicians to the *imagination*. What a wonderful power this Imagination must be, to be the sole cause of so many extraordinary effects! Among its other virtues—which the physicians have not noticed—it seems to provide an excellent refuge for ignorance and laziness. But if the imagination really does possess such astonishing powers, why, in the name of common sense, do doctors not prescribe Imagination to their patients more often, instead of poisonous drugs? Is there more quackery in curing diseases using the Imagination than by using Rhubarb, Magnesia, Opium, and Arsenic? It is highly probable, if not absolutely certain, that the discovery of that organic susceptibility which gave rise to magnetic treatment did not originate entirely with Mesmer himself, but was suggested to him by reading the works of certain mystical writers of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, to which reference has already been made. But Mesmer has the unquestionable merit of being the first in recent times who made use of the hints provided by these earlier writers, and who, through patient and tireless investigation and experiment, succeeded in establishing as demonstrated fact that which, as far as we know, had previously been, at least in a great measure, theory and conjecture.

From the time of this curious discovery, however—in whatever manner it may have been suggested—its author daily assumed a more mysterious demeanor, veiled his experiments and observations in a kind of sacred obscurity, and spoke no longer of mineral, but of *animal magnetism*. He no

I formerly mentioned that, for this and other reasons, many intelligent persons believe the name "Animal Magnetism" to be improper; but it would not be easy now to substitute one more appropriate.

No person was able to penetrate this mysterious obscurity; but it was still commonly believed that Mesmer continued to operate by means of magnetic rods concealed on his person. Meanwhile, some learned individuals endeavored to discredit his treatment; and others, who had once been associated with him, later publicly and explicitly proclaimed their skepticism. Mesmer, in short, was generally considered to be an impostor or, at least, a self-deceiving enthusiast. In order to counter these suspicions, he sent circular letters to the most celebrated learned societies in Europe, in which he attempted to explain his principles and gave an account of his magnetic cures. The poor reputation he now held in the eyes of his professional colleagues and the scientific public in general induced Mesmer to leave Vienna in the year 1777 to look for a new arena for the exercise of his magnetic art. Some time passed before the public received any certain news regarding his movements; but at length, in February 1778, he appeared in Paris. There, however, he initially found the learned community little inclined to patronize his discovery. Later, however, he was fortunate enough to convert Dr. D’Eslon, who became a zealous supporter of the magnetic doctrine and treatment. D'Eslon encouraged Mesmer to publish a short treatise the following year,† which, in addition to an apology for his conduct in Vienna, contained a summarized view of his system in twenty-seven propositions. This novel, extraordinary, and obscure theory found no favorable reception among men of science in France; on the contrary, it was, perhaps not undeservedly, treated as the dream of a visionary, with coldness or contempt.

The Medical Faculty of Paris, however, could not be expected to continue altogether indifferent to the subject, especially as one of its members, Dr. D'Eslon, was not only a zealous partisan of Mesmer, but had actually published a work upon Animal Magnetism. But the measures at length resorted to, for the purpose of vindicating the honor and privileges of the body, were not, assuredly, very creditable to the state of science and liberality towards the conclusion of “the philosophical century.” Instead of candidly investigating the whole matter, with a view to ascertain the truth or falsehood of the obnoxious doctrine, they proceeded, at once, to deprive the magnetic Doctor of his voice in the Faculty for a whole year, and threatened further, that, if he did not recant his principles at the expiration of that period, his name should be finally erased from the list of members; in short, that he should be excommunicated. An incipient schism in the church, some centuries ago, could not have been viewed in Rome with greater horror and alarm than that shown by these followers of Aesculapius upon the revelation of the magnetic heresy.*

But although deprived of scientific and profes-

---

<note>* Learned institutions rarely receive much credit from future generations for their attempts to interfere with the progress of scientific discovery. In the year 169, the celebrated Galen came to Rome, where he became famous for his successful practice; but the ignorance of the *learned* of those times drove him away with an accusation of practicing the magical arts. For a considerable period, the system of Copernicus was embraced only by astronomers; the learned in all other sciences viewed it with scorn and contempt. In the 17th century, Galileo was persecuted by the Roman Consistory for maintaining the true theory of planetary motions. The medical faculty has always been particularly unfortunate in its ridiculous crusades against unconventional remedies. Whenever they have ventured to challenge them, they have almost always been defeated. In the year 1566, the Faculty of Medicine at Paris issued an order prohibiting the use of antimony, and this order was confirmed by Parliament. Paumier of Caen, a great chemist and celebrated physician in Paris, having disregarded this order of the Faculty which was sanctioned by Parliament, was demoted in 1609. Quinquina, or Peruvian bark, was imported into Europe by the Spaniards in 1640. Nine or ten years later, the Jesuits distributed a large quantity of it in Rome, curing intermittent fevers with it as if by enchantment. The physicians, however, declared war against this effective remedy, and the church officials prohibited sick persons from using it, claiming that it possessed no power except what it derived from a pact made by the Indians with the devil. In 1784, the Medical Faculty of Paris prohibited the practice of Animal Magnetism by any of its members, under the penalty of being stripped of the privileges of their profession.</note>

### The very mystery in which Mesmer shrouded his treatment tended to excite curiosity, while it diverted attention from the active principle; thus, it caused him to be regarded individually as an extraordinary figure, full of ancient Egyptian wisdom and familiar with all the secret influences of nature. While this extended his reputation, it also seemed to flatter the man’s vanity and mystical disposition. His house became crowd-

<note>...others, all enlightened and talented men. M. de Ségur never abandoned his conviction regarding the reality of the phenomena of Animal Magnetism, and he very judiciously appeals to his own experience to justify this conviction. "I have no desire," he says, "to enter into any controversy on the subject; it is enough for me to affirm that, having been present at a great number of experiments, I have witnessed impressions and effects that were very real and very extraordinary, but for which I have never had the cause explained." Regarding the supposition that these impressions and effects may be the results of a heightened *imagination*, M. de Ségur very appropriately asks whether this word *imagination* can be considered a sufficiently satisfactory refutation, and whether the learned and philosophical are not bound, at least by the love of truth, to investigate the causes of this new and strange power of the imagination. Assuredly, he says, when such men as I have mentioned, and hundreds of other learned and intelligent individuals throughout Europe have expressed their conviction in the reality of certain facts based on personal experience, it must require something more than a mere theoretical refutation to invalidate the evidence in favor of a particular doctrine. It is not enough to attribute the effects in question to the influence of the imagination; the supporters of that theory are urgently called upon to explain what they mean by imagination, and how these peculiar effects can be rationally attributed to the influence of that faculty.</note>

# CHAPTER XI.

ALTHOUGH Mesmer had the unquestionable merit of being the first who experimentally discovered and demonstrated the effects of the magnetic process upon the animal constitution, and who employed that process systematically for the cure of diseases, it cannot be denied that he greatly delayed the general acknowledgment of the reality and the value of his discovery by the absurd affectation of much pointless, unnecessary, and almost ludicrous solemnity in his mode of conducting the treatment. We have now no means of ascertaining whether all this was done merely for the purpose of *mystification*, or whether he himself actually believed it to be essential to the success of his practice. There can be no doubt, however, that this affectation of mystery was highly unfavorable to the scientific investigation of the subject, besides injuring his own character in the eyes of many learned and sensible persons, who, looking only at the accessories and having no knowledge of the essential agent, were disposed to regard him mere-

He operated not only by the actual touch of his hands, or by means of an iron rod extended to some distance from his body; but, by means of cords, he placed his patients in connection with magnetized trees, or conducted the invisible magnetic fluid out of covered vessels (*baquets*) to the patients, who sat around in a circle; and, by this treatment, he was able to throw them into very peculiar states, which could not be properly called either sleeping or waking, but presented some of the phenomena of both. It sometimes happened, however, that none of these arrangements were found necessary; for a single look from Mesmer was frequently sufficient to produce the same effects. This last circumstance will be better understood when we come to consider the improvements which were made upon the processes of <term>Animal Magnetism</term> after the retirement of its discoverer.

These men, upon a superficial view and judging merely from what was actually presented to their senses, must have been inclined to attribute any effects they witnessed to the influence of the surrounding scene upon the imagination and the nervous system, rather than to that secret <term>magnetic virtue</term> to which the operator ascribed them, but which could not be visibly demonstrated.
