Mesmer was not only deprived of the support of the medical profession and the protection of the government; he was ridiculed by the wits of Paris, and attacked and slandered by the public journals, into which, we are told, the censors allowed no article to be admitted which originated from any of his partisans. Indignant at such narrow-minded conduct, he at length found it necessary to vindicate himself, and to expose to the world the unfair proceedings of his enemies.<note>See *Historical Summary of the Facts relating to Animal Magnetism, etc.* 1781; a work which deserves to be carefully read by all those who wish to obtain a full knowledge of the early history of the magnetic doctrines and practice, and of the violent struggle they had to maintain against prejudice and persecution.</note>

It cannot be denied, however, that Mesmer drew down upon himself a great deal of this censure and persecution by the obscurity of some of his propositions, the mystery attending his practice, and by the coldness and contempt with which he chose to treat the professors, as well as the profession, of the medical art. He boldly set out with the extraordinary and novel principle: <margin>⌝</margin> *There is but one health, one disease, and one remedy;* and he claimed for himself the discovery of the grand <term>panacea</term>.

<summary>Franz Mesmer faced significant opposition and censorship from the medical community and the press, though his own secretive and arrogant behavior fueled much of this hostility. To add to the unpleasantness of his situation, a misunderstanding arose around this time between him and his intimate friend and devoted partisan, D'Eslon, who had set up a separate and independent magnetic establishment—a step which caused a serious breach between the disciple and his master. The consequence of all these unpleasant circumstances was that Mesmer left Paris and went to reside for a time at Spa; until at length he was persuaded, by the requests of his friends, to return to the French capital for the purpose of delivering a course of lectures on his magnetic remedy.

Mesmer now resorted to a proceeding which has exposed him to a great deal of criticism. He had previously refused a very generous financial reward offered to him by the French government for the communication of his secret, under the pretext that knowledge of it might lead to dangerous abuses; whereas, upon his return to Paris at this time, he agreed to sell this secret—which he had declined to entrust to the prudence and discretion of the magistracy—to every private individual who was willing to pay one hundred Louis-d'or in return. With this view, he established a secret society under the name of “*The Harmony*,” where he initiated those who paid him the above price into his mystery, under the most sacred

In the meantime, however, some of Mesmer’s pupils made more prudent and cautious use of Animal Magnetism. They established *Harmonic Societies* in various provinces and towns of France, and joined together under the general supervision of Mesmer. In these institutions, the poor and sick were magnetized *for free*, in the presence of physicians; the discoveries made during their practice were shared with one another; and the most interesting cases were published in the press.<note>These early publications on the phenomena of Animal Magnetism are very numerous, and some of them are extremely interesting. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the 1784 French commissions, specifically addressing the critiques of their investigative methods and summarizing their final report on Animal Magnetism.</meta>

The whole of this investigation, however, is alleged by the professors of **Animal Magnetism**, and with good reason, to have been conducted in a manner that will sufficiently show the objective they appear to have had in view, and the method by which the investigation was conducted:

1. The fluid, which the Commissioners call the animal magnetic fluid, does not exist, because it escapes all the senses.

2. Since this fluid escapes all the senses, its existence can only be demonstrated by curative effects in the treatment of diseases, or by momentary effects on the <term>animal economy</term>. *The treatment of diseases must be excluded from these two proofs, because it can only provide results that are always uncertain and often deceptive.*

3. The true proofs—the purely physical proofs of the existence of this fluid—are *the momentary effects on the animal body.*

To confirm these effects, the Commissioners conducted tests: 1. On themselves; 2. On seven patients; 3. On four individuals; 4. On a group gathered at Mr. Franklin’s; 5. On patients gathered at Mr. Jumelin’s; 6. With a magnetized tree; 7. Finally, on various subjects.

4. From these experiments, the Commissioners concluded that imagination is everything, and that Magnetism is nothing. Imagination, imitation, and touch—these are the true causes of the effects attributed to Animal Magnetism.

5. Since the procedures of magnetism are dangerous, it follows that any public treatment where the methods of magnetism are used can only have disastrous effects in the long run.

Such is the substance of this celebrated report. It seems quite clear that these Commissioners were exceedingly ignorant of the subject they were charged to investigate, and that their report was addressed to a public even more ignorant than themselves. But, in other respects, the method pursued by the Commissioners in their inquiries was quite absurd. Every system of doctrine can be legitimately refuted only based on its own principles—namely, by disproving its facts and invalidating the principles deduced from them. Now, how did the Commissioners proceed? It was asserted by the magnetizers, based on alleged experience, that magnetic treatment was highly effective in curing diseases; but, as far as I am aware, they never pretended to say that the effects could always be produced instantaneously. But the Commissioners, with singular inconsistency, completely rejected the proofs resulting from the treatment of diseases for a reason which—if valid at all—is equally applicable to every kind of remedial treatment and would establish the total uncertainty of all medical science: namely, that "it could only furnish results that are always uncertain and frequently fallacious." Thus, they restricted their investigation to an examination of effects produced instantaneously, which formed no part of the magnetic doctrine.

The Commissioners, however, do not pretend to deny that some effects were produced during their experiments, which is indeed remarkable enough considering the circumstances in which they were conducted. But they ascribed these effects to imagination, imitation, and *attouchement*—that is to say, they attempted to refute one theory by setting up another of their own; and whether they were right or wrong is a matter of relatively little consequence. It is the facts, and not the opinions of theorists, which are of primary importance here, as in all other scientific questions. The commissioners, then, admitted that certain effects were produced by the magnetic processes which they attempted; and they even proposed a theory to account for the phenomena. But this theory must simply take its place alongside all the others which have been formed upon the same subject; and it must be ultimately accepted or rejected according to whether it is found to be confirmed or refuted by experience.*

During the active period of his career, Mesmer was exposed to a great deal of public resentment, and his character was frequently attacked by the most insulting slanders. But the important and now generally recognized facts which he brought to light through his practice prove that he was no impostor. He appears to have been naturally inclined toward mysticism; he presented his discovery with all the trappings of quackery; and his natural vanity constantly led him not only to exaggerate his own merit but to treat his opponents—and even his professional colleagues in general—with a presumptuous contempt that they could not fail to resent. Yet he seems to have been perfectly sincere in the doctrines he professed and honest in the details of the experience upon which his theory was founded. What can those who distinguish so sharply between Magnetism and Mesmerism—who present the significant ideas of this man as their own discoveries under new names (*Siderism* and *Tellurism*), or who merely correct one or two trivial errors—what can they answer when they are asked who it was that made them familiar with all they know of Magnetism? Who made them so wise that they are capable of justly criticizing its discoverer in one thing or another? The Pygmy stands upon the shoulders of the Giant, looks down upon him with contempt, and exclaims—*How tall I am!* Those ideas of the ancients may have given his mind its first impulse and direction; they may have led him, along the untrodden path, to the goal for which he strove and which he attained. But, even admitting that Mesmer derived the first idea of his theory and art from Maxwell or any other forgotten author, would that circumstance diminish his fame? All great men who have lived, or who live now, have been indebted to teachers and books for their knowledge; they increased that knowledge through their own experience and reflection. But can we justly deny them respect and merit because the foundation was laid by others? ## CHAPTER XII.

After the retirement of Mesmer, the practitioners of <term>Animal Magnetism</term> in France became divided into three different schools, which varied considerably from each other in their respective modes of treatment.

The original school of Mesmer, whose primary seat was in Paris, operated mainly by physical means: by touching, rubbing, and applying pressure with the hand, or by the use of metal conductors. His disciples used magnetic vessels (*baquets*<note>The *baquet* was a type of covered tub, filled with water, iron, glass, etc., which was supposed to contain the magnetic influence; cords were attached to this vessel for the purpose of conducting the magnetic power to the patients under treatment.</note>) and trees, as well as magnetized baths. They recommended drinking magnetized water and carrying magnetized plates of glass upon the stomach; in general, their treatment was designed to produce strong crises and reactions in their patients. They regarded the convulsions that followed as a healing process of nature; and, accordingly, they endeavored to bring

---

them through artificial means and called them *crises*. As the first and primary object in every magnetic treatment was to produce such crises, certain rooms, called *chambres de crise*, were prepared for the purpose; these were apartments where the walls and floors were covered with mattresses and cushions to prevent the convulsing patients from injuring themselves during the onset of their crises. Mesmer’s idea that light and sound are particularly favorable to the magnetic process has already been mentioned.

A second school was established at Lyons and Ostend under the direction of the Chevalier Barbarin, who adopted a mode of treatment totally different from the previous one.

The school of Barbarin operated in a purely psychological manner, admitting no other agents in the magnetic process than *faith* and *volition*. For this reason, its followers were known by the name of the *Spiritualists*. They practiced no specific manipulations; any physical operations they allowed were considered merely accessory or auxiliary, and by no means essential to the success of the treatment. They endeavored, therefore, to produce all the phenomena of Animal Magnetism in their patients through firm determination and by the energy of the operator’s volition, even at

The age of the magnetizer is also said to be a matter of considerable importance. To these physical qualifications must be added the psychological ones, consisting of a sound and energetic mind, a lively faith, and a determined, absolute will.

The magnetic treatment is either simple or compound. In the former case, the magnetizer operates solely by himself; in the latter, he makes use of certain external media. Simple magnetic treatment is usually administered with the hand, and is therefore called *manipulation*. But the magnetizer can also operate without employing the hand—by breathing, or by fixing his eyes or his thoughts, or both, steadily and intensely upon the patient. When the magnetic connection has been previously established, a single fixed look from the magnetizer, accompanied by energetic volition, has frequently been found sufficient to throw the patient into a state of magnetic sleep, or somnambulism.

The magnetic treatment by manipulation encompasses several modes of touching and stroking with the hand, which could not be described here in detail without leading us into *prolixity*.*

The usual method is to stroke repeatedly with the palms of the hands and the fingers in a downward direction, from the head to the feet; and, when returning the hands to the starting position, to move them in a semicircle while turning the palms outward, so as not to disturb the effects of the direct stroke. To magnetize in the opposite direction—that is, from the feet upward toward the head—not only counteracts the effects of the former method but frequently has a negative effect itself, especially in the case of irritable subjects. If we attempt to operate with the back of the hand, it is probable that no effect whatever will be produced upon the patient.

If, during this process, the hands or fingers of the operator actually touch the body of the patient, it is called manipulation *with contact*; if, on the contrary, the operation is conducted from some distance, it is called manipulation *in distans*. Manipulation with contact is of two kinds: it is accompanied either by considerable pressure or by a light touch—referred to as manipulation with *strong* or with *light* contact. Manipulation with *strong* contact is certainly the most ancient and the most universally prevalent mode of operating; and traces of it are to be found in

I must not, however, overlook the method of administering <term>Animal Magnetism</term> adopted and recommended by Professor Kluge, whose work describes the whole process with great detail.*

Before commencing the <term>magnetic manipulations</term>, it is necessary that the <term>magnetizer</term> and the patient should be conveniently placed; so that the former may be enabled to perform his operations freely, and the latter may be prepared for the expected <term>crisis of sleep</term>. A semi-reclining posture for the patient is, on the whole, the most convenient, with the body being bent enough that the operator can reach from the crown of the head to the toes without difficulty. If the patient is unable to leave his bed, we must try to place him in a properly bent position. It is not necessary for the patient to be completely undressed, except that no silk covering should be allowed to come between them.

# ANIMAL MAGNETISM.

The best position, perhaps, in which a magnetic patient can be placed, is in an easy armchair, with his hands resting on the arms, his feet upon a footstool, and his knees bent somewhat forward. The <term>magnetizer</term> then places himself upon a common chair, opposite to the patient, and so near as to be able to enclose the patient's knees within his own, but without intentionally touching them.

When the <term>magnetizer</term> has thus placed the patient and himself in the most convenient posture, he proceeds to the manipulations, which are distinguished into the *preparatory* and the *effective*. The preparatory manipulations were formerly called *placing in connection or affinity* (*mettre en rapport, en harmonie*); denoting that they were employed for the purpose of establishing such a sympathy between the nervous systems of the <term>magnetizer</term> and the patient as should render the subsequent operations more certain and effective.

Some <term>magnetizers</term>, and among others Wienholt, it is said, proceeded at once to the effective treatment, without any preparation. Kluge, however, strongly recommends a contrary method, and, apparently, with good reason; because, otherwise, especially in the case of very irritable patients, the preparatory manipulations enable them to endure the more effective manipulations, which, without

### CHAPTER XIII.

The effects produced upon the organism of the patient by the operations described in the preceding chapter are truly wonderful; and, considering the apparent inadequacy of the means employed, can scarcely be expected to be believed, except by those who have actually experienced or witnessed them. These effects are very various and may be divided into two classes. The first consists of those general effects which are produced upon the entire bodily frame, and which are not merely periodical but continue throughout the whole treatment. The second includes those which affect only some particular functions of the organism, and which are not constantly manifested, but only at certain times, and especially during the magnetic manipulations. These last may be reckoned among the particular effects of Animal Magnetism.

This classification, of which I shall presently give a summary, follows the order of the different degrees through which the patient has been observed to pass during the magnetic treatment.

The *first* degree presents no very remarkable phenomena. The intellect and the senses still retain their usual powers and sensitivities. For this reason, this first degree has been called the *degree of waking*.

In the *second* degree, most of the senses still remain active. Only the sense of vision is impaired; the eye gradually withdrawing itself from the control of the will. This second degree, in which sensitivity is partially disturbed, is, by some magnetizers, called the *half-sleep*, or the *imperfect crisis*.

In the *third* degree, all of the organs through which our communication with the external world is carried on (the senses) refuse to perform their respective functions, and the patient is placed in that unconscious state of existence which is called *magnetic sleep*.

In the former state, our knowledge is acquired through the use of certain intermediate organs of sense; in the latter, it appears to be obtained by means of some kind of more immediate intuition.

<note>In their state of *clairvoyance*, magnetic patients may be said to *feel*, rather than to *see*. Fischer's somnambulist assured him that he saw his internal parts, but not as if with eyes; however, he could not describe the manner in which he perceived them. Frederic Hufeland's patient said, only in the highest degree of lucidity, “*I see;*” at other times, she generally used the expression, “*I feel*” this or that part, this or that change, and so on. Gmelin's patient, too, said she did not *see*, but *feel*, and with great sensitivity, both internally and externally; and Scherb's patient declared that, in the magnetic sleep, the sensations were those of *feeling* rather than of *sight*; and that the feeling, during that state, was much more acute and delicate than when awake.—See KLUGE, pp. 283, 284.

A corroboration of these views may also be derived from the following curious declaration of Dr. Despine's cataleptic patient. “You think,” she said to those who had placed themselves *en rapport* with her, “that I do not know what passes around me every evening; but you are mistaken. I see nothing, but I *feel* something which makes an impression upon me, but which I cannot explain.”—See BERTRAND, p. 461, *Note*.</note>

## CHAPTER XV.

**SOMNAMBULISM** appears to have been known to the ancients, and has been noticed by Hippocrates, Aristotle, Galen, and others. It is only in the works of modern authors, however, that we find detailed and accurate descriptions of its phenomena.

Van Helmont tells us that, while at college, he slept in the same room as one of his comrades who was prone to somnambulism. This comrade rose during the night, took the key to the garden, and went walking in places where he ran the risk of falling; he then returned and replaced the key in a cupboard, just as he would have done when awake in broad daylight. One evening, Van Helmont took possession of the key without being noticed by his comrade and carefully hid it; but as soon as the other became a somnambulist, he went to look for it in the place where it had been hidden and took it without hesitation, as if he had placed it there himself.<note>Van Helmont, *De ortu Formarum*, section 52.</note>

Horstius, in his well-known work, relates that a young nobleman in the citadel of Brenstein was observed by his brother, who occupied the same room, to rise in his sleep, put on his cloak, and having opened the window, to climb, with the help of a pulley, to the roof of the building. There he was seen to tear a magpie’s nest to pieces and wrap the young birds in his cloak. He returned to his room and went to bed, having placed his cloak by him with the birds in it. In the morning he awoke and recounted the adventure as having occurred in a dream, and was greatly surprised when he was led to the roof of the tower and shown the remains of the nest, as well as the magpies hidden in his cloak. This individual would appear to have been in a state of imperfect somnambulism; otherwise, he would have remembered nothing of the circumstances when he awoke.

Henricus ab Heer mentions the case of a student at a German university who, having been very focused on the composition of some verses which he could not complete to his satisfaction, rose in his sleep and, opening his desk, sat down with great earnestness to renew his attempt. At length, having succeeded, he returned to bed after reciting his composition aloud and setting his papers in order as before.<note>The author remembers a somewhat similar circumstance,</note>

Several interesting cases of somnambulism can be found in Muratori's work, *Della forza della Fantasia Humana* (On the Power of Human Imagination), some of them given on the authority of Gassendi. One of Gassendi's somnambulists used to rise and dress himself in his sleep, go down to the cellar, and draw wine from a cask: *he appeared to see in the dark as well as in the clear light of day; but when he woke up either in the street or the cellar, he was obliged to grope and feel his way back to his bed. He always answered his wife as if he were awake, but in the morning he remembered nothing of what had passed.* Another sleepwalker, a countryman of Gassendi's, crossed a swollen torrent on stilts in the night, but upon waking, he was afraid to return before daylight or until the water had subsided.

The same author, on the authority of an eyewitness, Vigneul de Marville, gives the following account of the somnambulism of an Italian nobleman, Signor Augustin Forari:

The story of Lord Culpepper’s brother is quite well known. In 1686, he was indicted at the Old Bailey for shooting one of the Guards and his horse. He pleaded <term>somnambulism</term> and was acquitted after producing ample evidence of the extraordinary things he did in his sleep. There is a somewhat similar story of a French gentleman who rose in his sleep, crossed the Seine, fought a duel, and killed his antagonist, without recollecting any of the circumstances when awake.

# CHAPTER XVI.

The following case of somnambulism is reported in the 38th volume of the *French Encyclopedia*, on the highly respected authority of the Archbishop of Bordeaux, and has been frequently copied into other subsequent publications.

It is the case of a young priest who was in the habit of getting up during the night in a state of sleepwalking, going to his room, taking pen, ink, and paper, and composing and writing sermons. When he had finished one page of the paper on which he was writing, he would read over what he had written aloud and correct it. On one occasion, he had used the expression: *Ce divin enfant*. In reading over the passage, he changed the word *divin* to *adorable*. Noticing, however, that the pronoun *ce* could not stand before the word *adorable*, he added the letter *t* to it.

In order to determine whether the sleepwalker made any use of his eyes, the Archbishop held a piece of pasteboard under his chin to prevent him from seeing the paper upon which he was writing;

### CHAPTER XVII.

I am now about to present two or three cases of somnambulism, in which the condition appears to have been caused by, or at least accompanied by, an otherwise diseased state of the body. She then awoke, as if from a profound sleep, and when she perceived, from the appearance of the bystanders, that she must have had her fits again, she wept the whole day for shame, and never knew what had happened to her during the paroxysm.

This case bears considerable analogy to that of Louisa Baerkmann, reported by Dr. Joseph Frank, and noted in the Appendix (No. II). It tends, along with others, to demonstrate the total organic insensibility attending the condition, and the complete forgetfulness in the waking state of everything that occurred during the paroxysm.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

In some of the preceding cases, it must have been observed that the peculiar phenomena of somnambulism, although generally of a fairly uniform character, are more distinctly manifested in some instances than in others. Sometimes, too, only one or two of these phenomena are developed, while the others do not appear at all, or are only slightly noticed. These peculiarities may arise from the degree to which the patient is affected, from the opportunities afforded for experiment and observation, and from the knowledge and skill of the observers. But from the circumstance that a particular phenomenon has not been noticed in any one case, we are not entitled to conclude that it might not have been developed, had proper means been employed to ascertain its existence. It is only recently that professional men have obtained anything approaching an adequate knowledge of the nature of this condition, and of the best means of investigating the

<summary>This chapter introduction explains that the symptoms of somnambulism vary between patients and that the absence of a symptom in one case does not prove its impossibility. The author argues that medical understanding of the condition and the methods for investigating it have only recently begun to improve.</summary>

## CHAPTER XIX.

I shall cite only one other instance of natural somnambulism. The case is of recent occurrence. It is so extremely interesting in itself, illustrates so many of the characteristic phenomena of the condition under discussion, and was so carefully observed by a competent and skillful physician, that I am led to go much more fully into its details than I have done in the preceding instances. The following account is taken from a long and detailed report by Dr. Belden, the medical attendant of the patient, in the *American Journal of the Medical Sciences*, No. 28, for August 1834.

Jane C. Rider, seventeen years old and prone to frequent headaches, was first attacked with the unusual condition about to be described on the night of the 24th of June. Dr. Belden, who was summoned, found her struggling to get out of bed and complaining much of pain in the left side of her head. Her face was flushed, her head hot, her eyes closed, and her pulse much excited.

She then went into the pantry, where the blinds were shut and the door closed behind her. There, she skimmed the milk, pouring the cream into one cup and the milk into another without spilling a drop.

The above is a summary of the history of this very remarkable case—a case so carefully observed and so skillfully reported—a case in which, the intelligent reporter assures us, any idea of fraud or deception is ruled out. I have intentionally omitted all those details which would be interesting only to the medical student, and also many isolated circumstances and phenomena which seemed to me to be unimportant. I do not intend to investigate the theory by which the reporter attempts to explain some of the phenomena—namely, an excited state of certain parts of the brain. Until now, it has been too common a practice when treating this subject to build a theory upon a single, solitary fact or, at least, upon the circumstances of one individual case. In contrast, it seems to me much more philosophical and ultimately much more satisfying to first gather a sufficient collection of well-verified cases to establish a proper basis for induction <note>The process of deriving general principles from particular facts or instances.</note>, and then to proceed to classify the phenomena that may be found to have occurred in all, or in the majority of, instances.

## CHAPTER XX.

With the preceding case, I had originally intended to conclude my examples of natural somnambulism, believing that, with the magnetic cases to be presented later, I would have laid a sufficient foundation for a generalization of the phenomena. The following is the case referred to:

On the Serra de Piedade, the traveler says, I saw a woman of whom I had heard much in the Comarcas of Sabará and Villa Rica. Sister Germaine, the woman in question, was attacked around 1808 by a hysterical affliction, accompanied by violent convulsions. She was at first exorcised—remedies ill-suited to her complaint were used—and her condition degenerated from bad to worse. At length, at the time of my visit, she had for a long time been reduced to such an extreme state of weakness that she was no longer able to rise from her bed, and she lived on a diet that could scarcely have supported the life of a newborn infant. Her stomach was no longer in a condition to receive meat, rich soups, or gravies. Sweets, cheese, and a little bread or flour constituted the whole of her food; she was frequently unable to keep down what she had eaten; and it was almost always necessary to use considerable persuasion to convince her to eat at all.

It was universally admitted that Germaine’s manners had always been pure and her conduct irreproachable. During the progress of her disorder—

order, her devotion had daily taken on a more enthusiastic character. On Fridays and Saturdays she fasted completely; at first, indeed, her mother opposed this practice; but when Germaine declared that, during these two days, it was utterly impossible for her to take any nourishment, she was allowed to have her own way, and accordingly, submitted, on those occasions, to total abstinence. In order to indulge her devotion for the Virgin Mary, she had herself taken to the Serra de Piedade, where there is a chapel built under the auspices of Our Lady of Pity, and she obtained permission from her spiritual director to remain in this sanctuary. In this retreat, while meditating one day on the mystery of the Passion, she fell into a kind of ecstasy: her arms grew stiff and were extended in the form of a cross; her feet were positioned in the same manner; and in this position she remained for forty-eight hours. This was four years ago; and ever since then the phenomenon was repeated weekly. She returned to her ecstatic state on Thursday or Friday night, and continued in a sort of trance until Saturday evening or Sunday, without receiving the slightest nourishment, and without speech or movement.

The rumor of this phenomenon quickly spread through the neighborhood; thousands of people of all ranks crowded to see it; it was declared

to be a miracle; Sister Germaine was regarded as a saint; and two surgeons of the province gave an additional impulse to the veneration of the people by declaring, in a written document, that her situation was supernatural. This declaration remained in manuscript but was widely circulated, and numerous copies of it were taken. Dr. Gomide, an able physician educated at Edinburgh, thought it necessary to refute the declaration of the two surgeons, and, in 1814, published at Rio de Janeiro (though without his name) a small pamphlet, full of science and logic, in which he proves, by a multitude of authorities, that the ecstasies of Germaine were merely the effects of catalepsy.

The public was now divided in opinion; but crowds of people still continued to ascend the Serra to admire the miracle occurring there. Nevertheless, Father Cypriano da Santissima Trindade, the late Bishop of Marianna, a prudent, enlightened man, aware of the inconveniences which might arise from the numerous assemblies collected by Sister Germaine upon the mountain, and desirous of discrediting the pretended miracle—from which there resulted at least as much scandal as edification—prohibited the celebration of mass at La Piedade, under the pretext that permission had never been obtained from the king. and was supported by a stool. Her hand felt extremely cold, the thumb and forefinger were extended, but the other fingers were bent, the knees drawn up, and the feet placed over each other. In this position she was perfectly immovable; and her pulse being scarcely perceptible, she might have been taken for a corpse, if the rise and fall of the bosom in the act of breathing had not indicated the presence of life. I sometimes attempted to bend her arms, but without success; the rigidity of the muscles increased in proportion to my efforts, which could not have been more violent without causing discomfort to the patient. Certainly, I more than once closed her hands; but on releasing the fingers they resumed their former position."

Such is the case related by M. de St Hilaire, which has called forth the sneers of the *Westminster* reviewer. As I have already stated, it constitutes one instance, among many, of a specific variety of that organic condition which I have been attempting to illustrate under the generic name of Natural Somnambulism. It presents a specimen of catalepsy combined with devotional ecstasy, of which many other instances might be cited, were I not afraid of trespassing too much upon the time and patience of my readers.

Now, credulity and superstition, in one form or another, are probably fairly equally distributed across the globe—witness the followers of Joanna Southcote,* and the experts in unknown tongues among ourselves, and the recent case of Robert Matthews, or Mathias, in America. But if in search of ignorance, the reviewer certainly did not need to travel quite so far beyond the boundaries of Westminster. If the pious Brazilians were mistaken in supposing that there was anything miraculous in the case of Sister Germaine, the reviewer is even more unpardonably wrong in treating a natural occurrence with ridicule, and in describing <term>Animal Magnetism</term> as "a voluptuous trickery." competent knowledge of the literature and science of the age, should not be aware that the case described above constitutes one of a fairly numerous class, the phenomena of which have occasionally attracted the attention of physicians and philosophers. It is part of the business of <term>Animal Magnetism</term> to collect and classify these cases, and, if possible, by means of generalization and induction, to explain their peculiarities, to point out the natural principles upon which they depend, and thus deprive them of their miraculous character. In this interesting philosophical investigation, it is quite provoking to be met at every corner by the silly sneers of ignorance, imbecility, and an irrational incredulity.
